title: Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2014
short_title: Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill is part of a package that also includes the Health and Other Services (Compensation) Care Charges (Amendment) Bill 2014.

The package would change aged care funding by redirecting money from a workforce supplement into general subsidies for providers, and would allow a new online portal to use Medicare identifiers to verify client identities.
The package would also fix a problem in recovering past care costs for home care when a recipient gets compensation, making the rules the same as for residential care.
changes: The bill would remove the workforce supplement from the list of supplements that can be given under the subsidy principles of the Aged Care Act 1997.
The bill would change the Healthcare Identifiers Act 2010 to let data be collected, used and disclosed for the My Aged Care portal.
The bill would make minor clarifications and technical fixes to aged care and health laws.
summary.affected: Providers of residential, home and flexible aged care, aged care clients, and the Commonwealth.

speeches.speaker: Kevin Andrews
speeches.brief: Moved a companion bill to fix an anomaly allowing the recovery of past residential care costs but not home care costs from compensation payments, introduced separately from the main bill to comply with section 55 of the Constitution.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Supported most of the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2014 including the 1 January 2015 rollout of the My Aged Care gateway, but sought to amend provisions removing Labor's aged-care workforce supplement, citing the 2010 Intergenerational report's finding that a 300 per cent increase in aged-care workers will be needed by the middle of the century.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: Defended the government's changes to aged care funding, arguing that redirecting the $1.5 billion Aged Care Workforce Supplement back to providers was fairer than Labor's centrally planned scheme, and that the dementia supplement had blown out tenfold in cost, while highlighting that Tasmania has the largest and fastest growing aged population of any Australian state.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Opposed the government's cuts to Labor's $1.2 billion aged-care workforce supplement, which was designed to lift pay and conditions for around 350,000 aged-care workers from 1 July 2013, noting up to 90 per cent of those workers are women over the age of 45 working part time.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: Supported the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill, noting her electorate of Ryan has 13 nursing homes and care facilities, and criticised Labor's $1.5 billion Aged Care Workforce Supplement for only benefiting workers covered by an enterprise bargaining agreement, effectively pressuring them to join a union.

speeches.speaker: Terri Butler
speeches.brief: Opposed the redirection of Labor's $1.2 billion aged-care workforce supplement, which had aimed to lift pay for around 350,000 workers, disputing government claims it was tied to union membership, and cited the Productivity Commission's prediction that Australia will need three times its existing aged-care workforce by 2050, noting a 2011 census finding that 49 per cent of aged-care registered nurses were aged 50 or older.

speeches.speaker: Keith Pitt
speeches.brief: Supported the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill, detailing $1.1 billion flowing to providers between 2013-14 and 2016-17 and a $54 million boost for regional and remote aged care benefiting over 950 services, and highlighted that in his Wide Bay region 630 funded residential care beds remain unbuilt.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Criticised the Abbott government's aged-care and pension record after one year in office, citing independent research showing changed pension indexation would leave the average pensioner about $80 a week worse off over the next decade, and referenced the Productivity Commission's Caring for older Australians report, tabled in June 2011, which found the proportion of Australians over 65 would rise from close to 15 per cent now to about 24 per cent by mid-century.

speeches.speaker: Dan Tehan
speeches.brief: Supported the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill, welcoming a 2.4 per cent increase in care funding for eligible aged-care programs and a $54 million funding boost for regional, rural and remote providers through a 20 per cent increase to the viability supplement, both effective from 1 July 2014, and argued repurposing the workforce supplement avoided centralised control of the sector.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: Supported amendments criticising the government for cutting $653 million from the aged-care payroll tax supplement without consulting the sector, and for mismanaging aged-care funding, pointing to oversubscription of the Dementia and Severe Behaviours Supplement alongside undersubscription of the Dementia and Cognition Supplement and the Veterans' Supplement.

speeches.speaker: Amanda Rishworth
speeches.brief: Supported amendments to the aged-care bills requiring that the $1.1 billion being redirected to providers under this legislation actually be spent on workforce pay and conditions, criticising the government's June 2014 decision to abandon both the $653 million Aged Care Payroll Tax Supplement and the Dementia and Severe Behaviours Supplement without guaranteeing the funds would benefit workers.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: Supported the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill as important for his Lyne electorate, welcoming the repurposed workforce supplement for local facilities in Wauchope and Taree, and expressing hope that Nambucca Valley Care would take over an ageing aged-care facility in Gloucester.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill's redirection of the $1.1 billion aged-care workforce supplement, warning it would deny a promised 1.25 per cent pay rise to 350,000 aged-care workers like Heather, a Blue Care personal carer, and criticised the axing of a $653 million aged-care payroll tax supplement and the dementia and severe behaviour supplement.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Sought leave to adjourn debate on the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2014 until the following week, noting other members were ready to speak in the adjournment debate.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Argued against the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill, saying it would abolish the $1.1 billion aged care workforce supplement and dump the $16.15 a day dementia supplement introduced by Labor, warning this would leave aged care residents worse off as staffing levels struggle to keep pace with an ageing population.

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: Argued in support of the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill and the Health and Other Services (Compensation) Care Charges (Amendment) Bill, saying they would support stage 2 of the aged care gateway and online portal and allow recovery of past home care costs where a care recipient receives a compensation payment.
